A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JointDiff study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory-generation experiments, ablations, attention analyses, and a 15-participant NBA human evaluation in Appendix D.2.1.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds trajectory–event consistency measurements, further ablations, and an NBA12/13 forecasting comparison.

M1.justification: The proposed Gaussian–multinomial diffusion model, joint loss, CrossGuid conditioning, and hybrid sampler remain unchanged. Two residual blocks were already documented in v1's Appendix B. The absorbing-state and alternative T5 configurations are experimental variants rather than replacements for the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2.4 adds an evaluation named NBA12/13, but the PDFs do not explain its underlying data relationship to the existing NBA and Basketball-U datasets. Thus, expanded represented data or task coverage cannot be reliably distinguished from an additional forecasting protocol. The established sports datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds NRI, dNRI, FQA, Social-GAN, and GRIN to the reported NBA12/13 comparison in Table 6. It also introduces an absorbing-state JointDiff comparator across the existing sports generation settings in Tables 3 and 11. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives; previous comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include NBA12/13 minimum errors over 100 modes, consistency accuracy comparing generated events with possession inferred from generated trajectories, guidance-weight sweeps, and three T5 sizes. The absorbing comparison specifies an absorption rate of 0.01. Existing benchmark splits, training budgets, and 20-mode evaluations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendices D.3.3–D.3.5 add direct trajectory–event consistency analysis, multinomial-versus-absorbing tests, guidance-strength sensitivity, and text-encoder-size ablations. Existing scheduler, loss-weight, architectural, attention-entropy, and failure-case analyses remain. The human evaluation is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The human-study participant and comparison counts are unchanged. The new 100-mode evaluation is a sampling-budget choice, not additional uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All seven original tables retain their numerical results after matching renumbered tables. v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3, 6, and 9–11: for example, NBA12/13 minimum SADE/SFDE is 1.36/2.52 feet versus GRIN's 1.72/3.59, and unconditioned NFL average consistency is 0.86 versus 0.80 for absorbing diffusion. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 corrects the posterior-transition condition accompanying Equation 17 from s ≥ 1 to s ≥ 2, separating it from the final-step categorical prediction. The main factorization assumptions, loss derivation, and remaining mathematical development are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint continuous–discrete generation, WPG/text controllability through CrossGuid, a textual sports benchmark, and strong scene-level performance. The rewritten contribution list emphasizes capabilities already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 explains the absorbing comparator's weaker consistency through irreversible unmasking and links generation quality to consistency. It also interprets guidance-strength results and tentatively attributes T5-Large's weaker performance to embedding compression. Existing limitations concerning sparse events, limited text data, and NFL actor-assignment heuristics remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies zero-tensor conditioning dropout and RTX A6000 training hardware, documents the absorbing comparator's implementation source and parameter, and adds a project-page link. Most architecture, preprocessing, and training details were already present. The PDFs retain the prospective code/data release commitment.

R1.justification: Related work adds trajectory-modeling and robotics references and sharpens distinctions from Zeng et al.'s sequential event forecasting and absorbing-state diffusion. This refines the rationale for simultaneous, controllable multinomial generation while retaining the original research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted rewrites to contributions, related work, and the human-evaluation narrative, moves the human study into Section 5.1, and adds consistency and ablation subsections. Terminology, grammar, and publication headers are updated, while most existing methodological and appendix prose remains.

P2.justification: v2 adds five experimental tables, redraws the overview and architecture diagrams, enlarges and crops qualitative panels, and revises plot labeling. The unchanged human-evaluation histogram moves from the appendix into the main text. These substantially revise the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Section 5.3 and Tables 3 and 11 address an important validation gap in v1 by directly testing agreement between generated trajectories and events and comparing multinomial with absorbing diffusion. Guidance and encoder ablations further substantiate design choices. Together, these substantially strengthen the evidence for coherent joint generation while preserving existing results. Repeated-run uncertainty remains unreported.
